# Discussion

Ground-based time-lapse imagery allowed us to map 9-year changes in *Sasa* on an alpine slope at 1 m resolution and to fit models and project expansion at the scale at which it occurs. Three findings emerge. First, *Sasa* expanded, but more modestly than the gross expansion figure alone suggests: net change was +19% over 9 years. Nearly half of the apparent loss was exchange with dwarf pine, and the interpretation of this exchange remains unresolved. Second, although snowmelt regime was among the strongest environmental predictors in both models, establishment probability was most strongly associated with proximity to existing patches. Environmentally suitable area far exceeded occupied area, suggesting that dispersal limitation, rather than a shortage of suitable habitat, accounts for the gap. Third, process-based projections calibrated to the observed 9-year change indicated approximately 5,000–6,000 m² of spatially restricted establishment by 2030, concentrated in snowbed communities adjoining current patches and only modestly sensitive to earlier snowmelt. We discuss these findings in turn, followed by the role of the method, its limitations, and conservation implications.

## Magnitude and nature of the observed change {#sec-disc-change}

The distinction between gross expansion, gross loss, and net change is substantive. Gross expansion of 48% and net change of +19% describe the same 9 years; the difference comprises 2,468 cells classified as *Sasa* in 2012 but not in 2021. Of this loss, 47% was to dwarf pine and 38% to other vegetation; the three deciduous shrub classes (rowans, maple, and montane alder) accounted for only 15%. How should transitions to dwarf pine be interpreted? Dwarf pine is a prostrate, slow-growing conifer with annual shoot extension of only approximately 4–5 cm [@Amagai2015EcoRes]. Lateral advance over 9 years would amount to at most approximately 0.5 m, less than a single 1 m cell, making extensive concealment of *Sasa* stands by dwarf pine unlikely. Dwarf pine stands on the study slope are themselves expanding [@Amagai2015EcoRes], however, and their edges interdigitate with *Sasa* at sub-cell scales. Two mechanisms are therefore consistent with the data: lateral growth of dwarf pine branches into boundary cells and shifts in the classification of mixed pixels near boundaries. Indeed, 87.5% of *Sasa*→dwarf pine transition cells directly adjoined dwarf pine present in 2012 (median distance 1.0 m), and isolated transitions at least 5 m from the front accounted for only 1.6% of transition area (19 m²; Supplementary Information). Thus, almost all apparent loss to dwarf pine was a boundary phenomenon. The blind interpretation of paired images could not distinguish lateral growth from shifts in classification, however. Judgement distributions for loss cells were almost identical to those for stable controls (@sec-res-change), and the fate of individual 1 m cells could not be resolved at the photographic scale. The interpretation as a boundary phenomenon therefore rests on the concentration of adjacent transitions and the constraint imposed by dwarf pine growth rates. Accordingly, we treat loss area as an upper bound on true decline and net change as a conservative estimate of expansion. In contrast, transitions to other vegetation may include genuine local retreat and warrant targeted field verification.

The observed rate, +19% across the slope over 9 years (approximately 2%/year), lies at the lower end of plot-based estimates from nearby Murodo-daira, where *Sasa* patches expanded by 44–260% over 38 years [@Yoshida2016SasaTateyama]. In the Daisetsuzan Mountains, *Sasa kurilensis* cover in snowbed meadows reportedly increased by up to 47% over 32 years, with fronts advancing at a mean of 39 cm/year and a maximum of 50 cm/year [@Kudo2011EcoEvo]; on an annual basis, our observations are of similar magnitude. Continuous mapping across the slope reproduces the direction and order of magnitude reported by plot studies while adding spatial structure that plots cannot provide: where fronts move and where they remain stationary.

## Roles of dispersal limitation, environment, and snowmelt {#sec-disc-drivers}

Distance from the existing front dominated the establishment model. The 9-year establishment probability declined from approximately 10% within 5 m of the front to below 1% beyond 10 m, and the fitted kernel closely matched observed establishment rates by distance band. This distance scale is also consistent with measured rates of *Sasa* rhizome elongation in the Daisetsuzan Mountains (mean 39 cm/year, maximum 50 cm/year [@Kudo2011EcoEvo]). The strong distance dependence offers a direct explanation for why environmental potential (Model A) exceeded occupied area across a broad range of thresholds, reaching approximately 16 times the occupied area at the TSS-maximising threshold. Taken together, this gap between suitable and occupied habitat and the slow advance of fronts are consistent with a non-equilibrium interpretation in which the current *Sasa* distribution has yet to catch up with its environmental potential. If suitable habitat has expanded first, for example in association with earlier snowmelt, and dispersal-limited fronts are still filling that space, a stronger association with proximity than with environment would be expected.

Environmental terms describe variation in the rate of expansion from these fronts. In both models, habitat suitability and establishment probability peaked at a snowmelt climatology of approximately DOY 170–175 (Model A peak 172; Model B peak 175) and declined towards both earlier- and later-melting sites. *Sasa* thus has a favourable snowmelt window, and many current fronts adjoin sites on the later-melting side of that window. This response is consistent with the mechanism proposed for Daisetsuzan populations, in which a longer growing season accompanies *Sasa* advance from dwarf pine margins into wetter, later-melting sites [@Kudo2011EcoEvo]. It is also consistent with snow-manipulation experiments indicating that snowmelt timing structures tundra and alpine plant communities through growing-season length, soil temperature, and moisture [@Wipf2010PolarRes; @Wahren2005GCB]. Snowmelt DOY is nevertheless a proxy for these covarying conditions and was measured, not manipulated, in this study. Modelled associations are not evidence of causality; separating direct snowmelt effects from those of soils and microclimate requires field measurements.

The snowmelt-window interpretation also explains the apparently unusual behaviour of the projections. Projected establishment was 17% greater under the point-estimate earlier-snowmelt scenario, but slightly lower under the extreme scenario. Sites immediately adjacent to the front, where establishment is concentrated, lie on the late-melting side of the window, so a moderate advance shifts them towards its centre, whereas a larger advance begins to move them beyond it. The response of expansion to snowmelt is therefore non-monotonic, and its sign depends on the position of the front along the snowmelt gradient. This result becomes apparent only when expansion is modelled as a process.

## Is *Sasa* expansion a form of shrubification? {#sec-disc-shrub}

Woody shrub expansion is among the best-documented vegetation responses to warming in Arctic and alpine tundra [@MyersSmith2011ERL; @Bjorkman2018Nature; @Carlson2017ERL]. Although *Sasa* is not a woody shrub, it behaves functionally like expanding tundra shrubs: it forms dense, tall, evergreen stands that exclude subordinate species [@Kudo2011EcoEvo], and snowbed vegetation recovers after *Sasa* removal [@Kudo2017AlpBot]. It differs from typical shrubs in two respects, however. First, rhizome expansion proceeds from existing fronts with a metre-scale dispersal kernel, making it more spatially predictable than the spread of shrubs that establish new nuclei through seed dispersal and, in principle, amenable to targeted removal at the front. Second, *Sasa* competes with dwarf pine, which is also expanding under warming [@Amagai2015EcoRes]. The bidirectional *Sasa*–dwarf pine exchanges in the transition matrix suggest that these two expanding taxa are partly replacing each other as well as snowbed vegetation. This interaction merits study in its own right rather than being treated solely as an observational complication.

## Ground-based cameras among vegetation monitoring approaches {#sec-disc-method}

The role of ground-based cameras in this framework is complementary to that of satellites. Satellite time series offer continuity over decades and comparability among regions, making them well suited to analyses of landscape-scale greening and range shifts. Ground-based cameras provide sub-metre resolution and daily revisits within a fixed field of view, matching the scale of processes underlying the changes observed by satellites: patch-front advance, the sequence of snowmelt within snowbeds, and community boundaries. Our study illustrates what becomes possible in this gap: an establishment model fitted at the resolution of the process. The limitations are also specific: a fixed oblique viewpoint, coverage of at most a few km², dependence on continuous imagery throughout the period of interest, and restriction to taxa distinguishable in photographs, such as large or phenologically distinctive plants, including *Sasa* and dwarf pine. The last limitation could be partly relaxed through field collection of training data.

## Limitations {#sec-disc-limits}

(1) *Two time points.* The establishment model was fitted to a single 9-year interval, and projections assume stationary annual establishment rates conditional on the covariates. Independent validation was limited to spatial block exclusion, which indicated that *where* establishment occurs can be predicted reasonably well in unseen areas (AUC 0.79–0.86), whereas errors in *how much* occurs are substantial (block-level ratios 0.7–2.0). (2) *Snowmelt trends.* A 10-year record cannot detect trends of plausible magnitude. The scenarios evaluate no change, the point estimate of the observed slope, and its lower confidence limit; they are not predictions of snowmelt itself. (3) *Patch rule.* Projections depend strongly on the assumption that new colonies contribute to expansion only after forming an established patch (>5 m²); removing this rule triples projected area. The biological rationale is given in @sec-models, but the threshold is not a measured parameter. (4) *Classification.* Map accuracy estimates are upper bounds (see @sec-sasa-change), and the *Sasa*–dwarf pine exchanges show that boundary pixels are the most uncertain parts of the maps. These are precisely the pixels that define the front. (5) *Environmental coverage.* Soil properties, soil temperature, and moisture were not measured. The strong distance term may partly absorb the effects of unmeasured, spatially structured variables. (6) *Seed dispersal.* The establishment model captures only rhizome expansion. Establishment from seed following flowering events [@Miyazaki2009JPlantRes; @Mizuki2014PLOS] bypasses the distance constraint, which is why environmental potential is presented as a separate risk stratum. Even when seeds arrive, however, germination and seedling establishment may impose constraints independent of dispersal.

## Conservation implications {#sec-disc-conservation}

Two practical implications follow. First, near-term risk is spatially concentrated and can be assigned to specific locations. Approximately nine tenths of expected establishment within herbaceous vegetation by 2030 falls in two snowbed communities on the Ministry of the Environment's vegetation map, the *Fauria crista-galli*–*Carex blepharicarpa* and *Anaphalis alpicola*–*Phyllodoce aleutica* communities, and lies within a few metres of existing patches. Removal or containment at patch fronts bordering snowbeds is therefore a high-priority candidate intervention; intervention costs and regrowth following removal were not evaluated here. Recovery of snowbed vegetation after experimental removal has been reported elsewhere [@Kudo2017AlpBot]. Second, the much larger environmentally suitable area, most of which is unreachable by rhizomes within the projection horizon, is where establishment from seed would matter. Targeted surveillance for new isolated patches after flowering events, rather than continuous monitoring of the entire slope, would be a proportionate response. The presence or absence of rare species within risk areas cannot be determined at the resolution of the Ministry's 1:25,000 vegetation map; field surveys are the natural next step.

More generally, this framework separates two questions that a single suitability map can conflate: where environmental conditions permit a species, and how far it can actually reach. It answers the latter with a process model calibrated to observed change. For species such as *Sasa* that expand at metre scales, fixed cameras make this calibration possible at the scale of the process itself. The same logic could apply to other expanding species in snowy environments where comparable image records are available.
